record.paper_title: Open questions in massive star research
record.original_question: Where are the pair-instability supernovae that theory robustly predicts from helium cores of roughly 60 to 135 solar masses, given that no observed supernova has yet been identified beyond doubt as a pair-instability supernova? Are such events being missed because low-mass pair-instability explosions from compact Wolf-Rayet or helium stars can be comparatively dim, because hydrogen-rich pair-instability explosions resemble bright Type II-plateau supernovae, or because their occurrence is strongly restricted by metallicity and cosmic epoch?

evidence.quote: However, as yet, no observed supernova has been doubtlessly identified as PISN.
Therefore, there might be PISNe not recognized as such amongst the observed Type II supernovae, which is are known to show a large diversity.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Stellar evolution theory robustly predicts that stars whose helium cores have masses in the range of approximately 60 to 135 solar masses end their lives as pair-instability supernovae (PISNe): thermonuclear explosions triggered when electron–positron pair production destabilizes the oxygen-rich core, completely unbinding the star. Despite this prediction, no observed supernova has been unambiguously identified as a pair-instability supernova. Address the following: account for the apparent absence of confirmed PISNe in current supernova surveys. In particular, determine to what extent each of the following mechanisms is responsible: (i) low-mass PISNe arising from compact Wolf–Rayet or helium stars may be intrinsically dim and hence under-represented in flux-limited surveys; (ii) hydrogen-rich PISNe may be photometrically and spectroscopically indistinguishable from bright Type II-plateau supernovae and therefore misclassified; (iii) the occurrence of PISN progenitors may be strongly suppressed by metallicity-dependent mass loss and limited to early cosmic epochs, so that the local detection rate is intrinsically very low. Quantify the relative contributions of these effects and identify the observational signatures that would allow a definitive identification of a pair-instability supernova.
artifact.status_search_result: As of 2025, no supernova has been unambiguously confirmed as a pair-instability supernova. Several candidates (e.g., SN 2007bi, SN 2018ibb, SN 2023vbw) and indirect chemical-abundance evidence from halo stars such as LAMOST J1010+2358 have been proposed, but the community continues to regard a definitive detection as lacking. Recent theoretical work (e.g., 2025 A&A study on stellar winds and PISN rates) still treats the question as open.

status_evidence.snippet: We still lack an uncontroversial detection of a PISN, even if several studies have reported possible candidates.

status_evidence.title: Researchers find evidence for a Pair-instability Supernova from a very massive first star
status_evidence.snippet: First definitive association of a Galactic halo star with an abundance pattern originating from a PISN.
status_evidence.claim: Indirect chemical evidence has emerged but direct supernova-level identification remains unestablished.
